paras: The attempted lynching at the Grayson County jail was a confrontation in Grayson County, Texas, reported in April 1903, in which an armed mob of about a thousand men twice demanded a Black prisoner held on an assault charge. Sheriff Lee McAfee refused to give him up, and the mob turned away. The story ran in the press as a tribute to the sheriff.
The prisoner, whose name was not given, was accused of assaulting a woman, knocking her husband senseless and beating the children. The Globe-Democrat said he was caught with blood on his clothes.

Armed with shotguns and Winchesters, a crowd described as "a thousand angry Texans" marched to the jail and demanded the prisoner. McAfee refused, saying it was his duty to hold the man for the court, and the mob backed down. At the examination hearing, the sheriff escorted the prisoner to and from the court room with "a picked band of deputies" while the mob waited "rope in hand."

After the hearing the crowd moved to the jail and again demanded the prisoner. McAfee told the men he would protect the prisoner at the cost of his life if need be, and that the man must have "a legal trial before twelve citizens." He added that he was willing for the prisoner to hang, "but he must be hanged legally," and the crowd turned away.
No report of a trial, a verdict or arrests of mob members was found, and the coverage gives no date for the confrontation.

The only account found is a feature headed "A Texas Sheriff," which the Ocala Banner of Florida printed on April 24, 1903, crediting the St. Louis Globe-Democrat. It opened with a portrait of McAfee at the Binkley House at Sherman and said he had "just made himself famous by standing out successfully against a mob." The piece praised the sheriff's courage and closed that "the majesty of the law was vindicated magnificently," yet it called the prisoner a "wretch" and a "brute" who "deserved quick death."
No report of the episode was found in the Black press.

reader.title: Attempted lynching at the Grayson County jail, Texas
bases: An armed mob marched on a county jail and twice demanded a Black prisoner held on an assault charge, standing 'rope in hand', and turned away when the sheriff refused (A1).

The mob of about a thousand men had no lawful authority and sought the prisoner over an alleged crime, but the sheriff kept him and no one was killed, so this was an attempted lynching, not a lynching (A1).
The only account is one feature story credited to the St. Louis Globe-Democrat and reprinted in the Ocala Banner; no local or wire report and no Black-press coverage was found (A1).

accounts.label: St. Louis Globe-Democrat feature (reprinted)
accounts.gist: A thousand armed Texans twice demanded a Black prisoner accused of assault; Sheriff McAfee refused, promised a legal trial and even to hang him legally, and the mob turned away.

framing.detail: Headed 'A Texas Sheriff', the piece celebrates McAfee for having 'saved a negro from summary vengeance' and the 'majesty of the law', yet treats the accusation as proven and says the prisoner 'deserved quick death'.

record_check.dossier: Undated; only known to be on or before 1903-04-24, the date of a reprint of a St. Louis Globe-Democrat feature; it may be weeks or months earlier
Grayson County jail; Sherman appears only as where the sheriff was sitting when interviewed, not as the place of the jail
Armed gathering and two demands at the jail, with a rope shown at the hearing; no attack on the jail is reported
The mob made two demands, one at first and one after the examination hearing, and turned away both times

info: Not stated; on or before 1903-04-24, when the reprint ran; the sheriff is described as having 'just' stood off the mob
The jail of Grayson County, Texas; the article places the sheriff at the Binkley House at Sherman but does not name the town of the jail
An unnamed Black prisoner, the target of the mob; not harmed
Accused of assaulting a woman, knocking her husband senseless and beating the children; the paper says he was caught in bloody clothes
A mob of 'angry Texans' armed with shotguns and Winchesters; no one named
The mob turned away; the prisoner stayed in custody to await trial. No report of a trial or its result was found

sources.paper: The Ocala banner (Ocala, Marion County, Fla.)
sources.note: 'A Texas Sheriff', credited to the St. Louis Globe-Democrat: Sheriff Lee McAfee of Grayson County twice refused an armed mob of about a thousand demanding a Black prisoner; no date, prisoner's name or outcome given.
quotes: Lee McAfee faced a thousand angry Texans and saved a negro from summary vengeance. If ever a wretch deserved quick death this one did.
Armed with shotguns and Winchester, the people marched to the jail and demanded the prisoner.
The mob stood waiting, rope in hand
I am willing he shall be hanged, but he must be hanged legally.
The cause was least worthy, but the majesty of the law was vindicated magnificently.—St. Louis Globe-Democrat.
